one_liner: Ahead-of-time compiler from mruby 3.0 bytecode to C via MLIR/EmitC; about 1.4x faster than the mruby VM on aobench.
what_it_does: Lightstorm takes a Ruby source file, compiles it to mruby 3.0 bytecode, lifts that bytecode into a custom MLIR dialect ('rite'), lowers it through the cf/func/arith/emitc dialects and prints a C file. You compile that C file with clang and link it against Lightstorm's bundled mruby static library and a small runtime main, producing a standalone executable. It is a command-line compiler (lightstorm hello.rb -o hello.rb.c), not a library or a drop-in Ruby interpreter, and it accepts only a small subset of Ruby.
how_it_is_fast: It removes the mruby interpreter's fetch/decode/dispatch loop by turning each bytecode op into a call to an always_inline C helper from lightstorm_runtime.c, which the generated file #includes, so the C compiler can inline and optimize across ops (integer/float fast paths for arithmetic and comparisons, falling back to mrb_funcall_argv for everything else). Two MLIR passes run before emission: a simple escape analysis ('EscapeAnalysisAtHome') that gives arithmetic results consumed only by other arithmetic ops a stack-allocated RFloat slot instead of a GC-heap float, and MLIR's standard common-subexpression elimination. Method sends, ivar access and object allocation still go through the regular mruby runtime, which is why instructions only drop about 12-21% on the chart.
when_to_use: Embedding mruby (for example a game scripting layer, the DragonRuby use case) and wanting to ship hot, float-heavy scripts as native code instead of bytecode.
Numeric loops written with while loops, plain methods and instance variables, which is exactly the shape of the aobench port it was tuned on.

Research or teaching: a compact (about 1,000-line bytecode converter) example of building a language AOT compiler on MLIR with the EmitC dialect, so the output is portable C rather than target-specific LLVM IR.
Targets where JIT is not allowed (consoles, iOS) but an extra C compile step in the build is fine.
when_not_to_use: Any normal Ruby program: the converter rejects blocks, lambdas, yield, rescue/raise, super, default, variadic, keyword and block arguments, OP_ASET and several other opcodes (lib/compiler/converter.cpp), so idiomatic code using .times or .each does not compile; the aobench port itself had its .times blocks rewritten as while loops.

CRuby/MRI workloads or Rails: it is built on mruby 3.0.0 (pinned submodule commit 0f45836) and its default gembox, not CRuby, and it is not compared against CRuby or YJIT at all; Spinel or TruffleRuby are the siblings to look at there.
Code that relies on Ruby exceptions: any exception raised inside a call made through ls_send_argv is caught, printed and the process calls abort().
Production use: version 0.1.0, no issues filed, no releases, last commit 2024-12-13, and only one benchmark published.

If you need a large speedup on call-heavy code: method dispatch is still mrb_funcall_argv without inline caching ('TODO: add caching' in the runtime), so gains are limited to removing dispatch and boxing overhead.

integration.dependencies: LLVM 19 with MLIR (find_package LLVM and MLIR), CMake 3.28+ and Ninja to build the compiler; bundled mruby 3.0.0 submodule (built with rake, so Ruby/rake is needed); hyperfine and Python 3 for the benchmark target; lit and filecheck for integration tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for the compiler; clang-19 (Ubuntu preset) or Homebrew llvm@19 (macOS preset); generated code is C compiled with clang
integration.platforms: Ubuntu and macOS build presets; generated C is meant to be portable, other OSes not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented (single mrb_state per program, as in mruby)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same mruby 3.0 runtime and semantics for the supported subset, but whole-program AOT to an executable; no runtime eval/require of new code and large parts of Ruby syntax rejected at compile time

gotchas: Harness flaw in the published benchmark setup: cmake/mruby.cmake builds the whole mruby library with CFLAGS set to LIGHTSTORM_CFLAGS, which is just '-g' unless LIGHTSTORM_LTO is set, and mruby's gcc/clang toolchain (tasks/toolchains/gcc.rake at the pinned commit) replaces its default '-g -O3' with ENV['CFLAGS'], so in the default configuration the baseline mruby VM (vm.c and the rest of libmruby.a) is compiled without optimization while the Lightstorm-generated C and its inlined runtime get CMake's Release -O3. The README chart does not say which configuration produced it, so the ~30% gain may partly be -O3 vs -O0 (from reading the build files; not reproduced here).

The escape-analysis pass only checks that every user of an arithmetic result is another arithmetic op; if that consumer falls back to a user-defined operator method (for example a custom Vec#* taking a Float argument), a pointer to a stack-allocated RFloat is passed into Ruby code that can store it, which would dangle after the function returns (from reading lib/optimizations/optimizations.cpp; not tested).

Arithmetic fast paths do not check whether Integer or Float operators have been redefined (the 'need to check if op is overridden' comment has no check behind it), matching mruby's own VM shortcuts but not CRuby semantics.

bench.py runs hyperfine on both executables without comparing their stdout, so the benchmark itself does not check that the compiled and interpreted aobench render the same image; the image is only 64x64 with 2 subsamples and 8 AO samples, so process startup (mrb_open with the default gembox) is part of the measured time.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Lightstorm over Spinel or TruffleRuby only if you are already on mruby (for example embedding it in a game) and can restrict hot code to its block-free subset; Spinel is the catalogued choice for big AOT speedups over CRuby (about 8.5x over YJIT on 28 benchmarks), and TruffleRuby or YJIT if you need full Ruby. Against LuaAOT, the closest analogue (AOT of a small embeddable VM's bytecode to C, 1.2x-2.6x over Lua), Lightstorm shows a similar size of gain but on one benchmark only.
verified_claims_summary: One first-party bar chart for the aobench Ruby port: total time about 78% of the mruby 3.0 bytecode VM for plain compiled output and about 71% with escape analysis plus CSE (about 1.4x faster, derived from page data), with cycles, instructions, branches, 'misses' and loads/stores also lower; the harness is hyperfine (one warm-up run) over the Lightstorm executable and the same program as mruby bytecode, built with clang 19, but CPU, run count and whether LIGHTSTORM_LTO was set are not stated. The LLVM blog post (blocked here; search snippet only) says other benchmarks ranged from 1% to 1200% speedups, but those numbers are not in the repo.
status_note: Stale since 2024-12-13 at version 0.1.0 with no releases or issues; MIT-licensed and small, so it is better read as a reference design for an MLIR/EmitC Ruby AOT compiler than adopted as-is.
